The use, or threat of use, of the veto may prevent the Council from responding to urgent situations and from acting on matters at the very heart of its mandate. We recall the importance of General Assembly resolution 76/262 in fostering transparency and accountability, and we encourage continued restraint in the use of the veto, particularly in cases in which the Council is called upon to prevent or respond to the most serious crimes of international concern or to address grave threats to international peace and security.

answer.markdown:
Several European States, speaking nationally and for groups, backed limits on the veto and fuller use of Article 27, paragraph 3, as when Italy said it “supports all initiatives that seek to impose self-limitations on the use of veto” in November 2025 [Source 1]. Countries from other regions went further or stressed reform, as when Malaysia said “the veto power must be abolished in the long run” [Source 17] in February 2025.

## Statements on behalf of groups

Groups of States speaking jointly called for restraint on the veto, particularly in cases of mass atrocities, as when the elected members’ statement delivered by Liberia said “we encourage continued restraint in the use of the veto, particularly in cases in which the Council is called upon to prevent or respond to the most serious crimes of international concern” [Source 21] on 19 August 2026.

- Speaking for the Benelux countries, Luxembourg’s Mr. Maes said the use and threat of the veto “are at the root of the Council’s paralysis” [Source 7] on 14 November 2025.
- Speaking for the Nordic and Baltic States, Denmark’s Ms. Lassen said “Permanent members should refrain from using it in cases of mass atrocities, including the crime of aggression” [Source 11] on 5 September 2023.

## European States

European Union member States speaking nationally supported the French-Mexican initiative and the ACT Group code of conduct, as when Lithuania said “We encourage all delegations to commit to the Accountability Coherence and Transparency code of conduct and the French-Mexican initiative.” [Source 4]

- Lithuania’s Mr. Pranevičius also said “The use, or rather abuse, of the veto power by Russia to shield itself from accountability for its illegal aggression against Ukraine cannot be ignored.” [Source 4]
- Spain’s Ms. Jiménez de la Hoz said both initiatives “should be incorporated into the Council’s rules of procedure” [Source 3] on 19 August 2026.
- Italy said it does not support expanding the category of permanent members, which “would inevitably generate additional vetoes” [Source 1].

## Asia, Africa and the Americas

Speakers from these regions backed restraint and accountability, with some seeking abolition or structural reform, as when Paraguay said “the veto should be formally abolished, limited or restricted, in particular in cases involving measures intended to prevent the most serious crimes or mass atrocities” [Source 8] on 19 August 2026.

- Singapore’s Mr. Gafoor said on 14 November 2025 that “the indiscriminate use of the veto has continued to affect the Council” [Source 10], with 17 vetoes since resolution 76/262.
- South Africa’s Mr. Van Schalkwyk said the resolution “has assisted” [Source 13] accountability, but that this “cannot replace the need for urgent Council reform” [Source 13].
- Egypt’s Mr. Mahmoud said on 24 October 2025 that reform should “grant new permanent members the power of veto and include two permanent African seats and permanent Arab representation” [Source 20].

## States of Oceania

Australia and New Zealand called for transparent, restrained use of the veto, as when Australia’s Mr. Larsen said “The veto is a powerful instrument, and its use must be transparent and restrained.” [Source 23]

- New Zealand’s Ms. Schwalger said on 26 January 2026 that the use of the veto “to prevent Council action... impacts every Member State.” [Source 24]

About the evidence: The records are Security Council statements from 2023 to 2026, mostly from working-methods debates, and do not include the permanent members. Several groups rest on only one or two speakers, so they should not be read as the position of every country in a region.
